beats.trigger: ## From Personal to Team
beats.got: nothing new

beats.trigger: The hard part is not access; it is absorption.
beats.got: Buying the tool is the easy part, and getting people to use it is where it fails. That matches my three programmes.

beats.trigger: Walk in with one example where people had access to a tool or process but real use did not follow.
beats.got: I have an example: the ERP reporting module nobody opened.

beats.trigger: **Interview** for your teammate's job-to-be-done using the agentic Jobs-to-be-Done pattern (Clayton Christensen and collaborators)
beats.got: nothing new. It is a list of verbs with no cost or payback attached.

beats.trigger: Hold that feeling. It's not a governance question yet. It's a generous one.
beats.got: nothing new. It asks how I feel, and I have no feeling about handing it over.

beats.trigger: Your teammate doesn't want your agent. They want a job done.
beats.got: Start from the colleague's task, not from the tool.

beats.trigger: The test is specificity: does it name one teammate, their current way of doing the job, and an outcome you could observe?
beats.got: The test is whether the output names a real person and something observable. I can check that.

beats.trigger: If the reason is merely *"we already have the platform,"* send it back.
beats.got: Don't pick a tool because we already pay for it. I have seen that in every IT decision here.

beats.trigger: You now have the teammate's job and a candidate selected against it.
beats.got: nothing new

beats.trigger: Now find the obstacle that decides whether the teammate can actually absorb it, then draft both halves of the plan.
beats.got: nothing new

beats.trigger: A good bottleneck explains why several other obstacles stay hard.
beats.got: Find the one constraint behind the others. That is how I read a P&L variance, so it is familiar.

beats.trigger: A polished technical file beside a people file full of unnamed roles is the finding, not a finished rollout.
beats.got: A plan with no owners is not a plan. It names the risk before I raise it, which I did not expect.

beats.trigger: checks the assumptions underneath these plans, imagines the failure
beats.got: nothing new

beats.trigger: The technical and people plans are hypotheses.
beats.got: The plans are hypotheses to test, not facts.

beats.trigger: what would have to be true for this teammate, doing this job, to fire their current hire and use my candidate?
beats.got: Ask what would make a person drop what they use today. It is a fair test, but I see no figure in it.

beats.trigger: Six months from now, the teammate went back to the incumbent.
beats.got: A pre-mortem that ends in one named person and one test. That is concrete enough to do.

beats.trigger: A candidate picked because it fits the infrastructure is shopping.
beats.got: Choosing by what is available is shopping, not design.

beats.trigger: The rest of this is about the person on the other end of it.
beats.got: nothing new

beats.trigger: The interview earned its keep when it found a third outcome past speed and quality: a dependency removed, an anxiety gone, a scope widened.
beats.got: Outcomes can be softer than speed and quality. I would want them measured.

beats.trigger: Hand someone the agent file and you have handed them the shell of a thing whose contents are still on your disk and in your head.
beats.got: The value sits in the builder's corrections and judgement, not in the file. That is a key-person risk.

beats.trigger: The fourth does not copy at all, which is why the product being sold as a shared agent is always three of the four parts
beats.got: Accountability does not copy. Vendors sell three of four parts and the fourth stays with whoever built it. Useful in a vendor negotiation.

beats.trigger: Many companies have rolled out access far ahead of trust.
beats.got: Licences are counted as one number, and that number is not adoption. It is my three failed programmes in two sentences.

beats.trigger: Michael Polanyi, a philosopher of science, had the line for it: *we know more than we can tell.*
beats.got: nothing new. A philosopher quote does not help my board case.

beats.trigger: In the full agent picture, this is the interface piece.
beats.got: It refers to earlier modules I did not do, so nothing I can use.

beats.trigger: Your candidate is not competing with nothing. It is competing with that.
beats.got: The rival is the spreadsheet and the habit, not another tool. Any business case has to beat the incumbent.

beats.trigger: Whether they pick it up is their decision, made for their own reasons, on a Tuesday you will not be in the room for.
beats.got: I can't force adoption. That is true, but it is also a bit soft.

beats.trigger: A missing name is a finding: it marks the part of this that is not built yet
beats.got: Empty owner fields tell me the programme isn't real yet. I can use that as a gate question: who owns this?

take_homes: Licences and access are not adoption. I should ask for evidence of use, not the number of seats.
A rollout plan with empty owner fields isn't a plan. I will ask 'who owns this?' before approving anything.
The competitor of any new tool is the spreadsheet or habit people use today, so the case must beat that.

monday.move: Ask my controller how the month-end variance commentary gets done today, step by step, and what it costs in hours. Then ask whether an agent could try one month. No tool change yet.
monday.stop_condition: If she can't give me hours and an owner for the current process, I drop it. A pilot with no baseline is not worth the time.
monday.blocker: IT has not approved the tool for finance data, and GDPR is untested. That would have to be cleared first.

misconception.why: The line about access running ahead of trust made me see that buying a licence is not the capability. People and owners are the capability. I would still call the licence the main cost until I see a number. The module gave me no cost or payback figure.

one_line: It says the right thing about adoption and missing owners, but I got no figure for cost or payback, and a lot of it was philosophy and talk about feelings.
